newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China dissident urges political exiles to leave HK.
newsitem.headline: China dissident urges political exiles to leave HK.

text.p: A leading Chinese dissident on Thursday warned fellow political exiles who fled to Hong Kong after Beijing crushed pro-democracy protests in 1989 to leave the British colony before it returns to China on July 1.

Han Dongfang, who founded an independent trade union during the 1989 demonstrations centred in Beijing's Tiananmen Square, said he trusted Hong Kong's post-handover leader Tung Chee-hwa but that exiles would not be safe in the territory.

While Han said he would stay in Hong Kong after the handover at midnight on June 30, dissidents who had crossed the border illegally during their flight from China would be at risk of arrest and should leave.

"I suggest those people who escaped to Hong Kong from mainland China...leave Hong Kong before that day. Don't stay here, because you will be in trouble," he told an audience at the Hong Kong Foreign Correspondents' Club.

China could use criminal charges based on border offences to arrest exiles, he said, adding that such action was unlikely to cause a strong reaction in Hong Kong because the targets would be from the mainland.
Human rights sources said in February that Western countries were prepared to grant asylum to around 40 dissidents and their families who were exiled in Hong Kong.

Fears among scores of such exiles have risen as Hong Kong's future leaders have unveiled plans to limit some political and civil liberties in the territory and to ban some "anti-constitutional" activities.

Han, a former railwayman who was jailed after the Chinese army crushed the 1989 pro-democracy protests, said he had confidence in Tung, who will lead Hong Kong after the end of 156 years of British colonial rule.
"I still trust him," Han said. "I don't think...he is going to destroy Hong Kong with his own two hands."
But Han added that some members of the Beijing-backed provisional legislature that will replace the current elected body were less benign.
The union activist, who has been blocked from returning to China, said he was in Hong Kong legally and would welcome the handover of sovereignty that would bring him back on to home territory.
China remained in urgent need of independent trade unions to protect workers, now represented only by state-run unions that worked for the interests of company managers and the government, Han said.
He said he expected to come under political pressure after the handover but had yet to decide how he would react.
"I'm just going to wait until they come," he said.
